contract.note: The contract requires an independent evaluation of DeepSearch reports specifically, which is fair. 'Reasonably often' and 'subtle' have no thresholds, so the result depends on interpretation.

attribution.note: Marcus's own stated lesson in his post.

semantics.note: The factual core is that polished LLM output often has subtle errors most people would miss. 'Caveat emptor' is a normative add-on and is not scored.

contract.note: The reading and period are ordinary. 'Most people wouldn't catch' is unquantified. The contract's lenient 'substantial share missed' test favours the speaker slightly, so I check the 'most' part separately.

evidence.note: BBC journalists found 51% of assistant news answers had significant issues (Dec 2024, published Feb 2025). Errors were common. It does not measure whether users detect them.
CHI 2024: 52% of ChatGPT answers were incorrect, and users missed the misinformation 39% of the time. That is frequent, but short of a majority.
Tow Center (Feb 2025) judged that a confident tone makes errors hard to distinguish. This is qualitative, and it was published just after the target period ended.

reviews.rationale: The evidence clearly shows that polished LLM output often contained errors in this period, so that part holds. That most people would not catch them is only partly shown: the best measure is 39% missed, and the other items are qualitative. The 'often errors' part holds; the 'most people' part is not established.
